title: Wiping the joints and leaving the reed on
summary: Hall describes his nightly routine of wiping the barrels and mouthpiece and leaving the reed on.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Reeds, mouthpieces and horns: the reed player's gear

blocks.x: I was wondering about, on a wooden clarinet, would you have to dry your joints, corks? No. No. Don't bother me.

The only thing like when I take my clarinet out at night, when I get ready to put in the case, I pull it apart. I run that piece of chamois through it. I pull the barrels off, you know, and wipe them on the inside. And I wipe my reeds, I clean my reeds off. I don't take the reed off, but I just stick it and run it through there and dry that mouthpiece.
Do you leave the reed on the mouthpiece? Yeah, I leave the reed. Some people say to keep it flat on something else. Yeah, they feel like when I clean my instrument.

Well, you don't have to take this part off. That fits in the case. But when you pull it off here, a lot of the time the water gets right in here. See, I wipe that out. And when you take this, I don't have to take this joint off every now and then. But when I take this mouthpiece off, I take my chamois and run it through here. But I don't touch the reed. No, I see. You leave the reed right on the instrument? I leave the reed right on the instrument and I clean that reed about every other day. I'll take it off because sometimes you take them off and it's plain good. When you put it back on, it don't look like it don't feel the same way. Sure. So when it's on that good and there's no trouble, you just leave it on. That's a good idea.
I have a lot of trouble. Yeah, when you put it back on.
A lot of times it's a good reed and you take it off too much and trying to put it back on, you mess it up. Take it to the right place. Yeah, that's right.
